content: Despite advancements in surgical techniques, the treatment of vulvar cancer through groin dissection is associated with significant morbidity. This morbidity is primarily linked to the invasive nature of the surgical procedure. In contrast, primary radiotherapy targeting the groin is hypothesized to result in reduced morbidity. However, the available evidence regarding the efficacy of primary radiotherapy, particularly in terms of groin recurrence rates and overall survival, remains inconsistent and inconclusive. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether primary radiotherapy to the inguinofemoral lymph nodes in patients with early-stage vulvar cancer is as effective and safe as surgical intervention. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies from 1966 to July 2010. An additional search in January 2016 did not identify any new trials. The inclusion criteria were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing inguinofemoral lymph node dissection with primary radiotherapy in patients diagnosed with early-stage squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies and extracted relevant data. The primary outcomes of interest were the incidence of groin recurrences, patient survival rates, and treatment-related morbidity. Among the twelve studies initially identified, only one small RCT involving 52 women met the inclusion criteria. The results of this single RCT suggested a trend toward higher rates of groin recurrence in the radiotherapy group compared to the surgical group, with a relative risk (RR) of 10.21 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.59 to 175.78). Additionally, disease-specific survival rates appeared to be lower in the radiotherapy group, with an RR of 3.70 (95% CI: 0.87 to 15.80). On the other hand, radiotherapy was associated with a reduced risk of lymphoedema (RR 0.06, 95% CI: 0.00 to 1.03) and fewer life-threatening cardiovascular complications (RR 0.08, 95% CI: 0.00 to 1.45). Patients undergoing primary surgery experienced longer hospital stays compared to those receiving radiotherapy, with an RR of 0.28 (95% CI: 0.13 to 0.58). The authors concluded that while primary radiotherapy to the groin is associated with lower morbidity, it may carry a higher risk of groin recurrence and reduced survival compared to surgical treatment. However, the findings of this study are limited by the small sample size and concerns regarding the adequacy of the radiotherapy technique used. Larger RCTs employing standardized radiotherapy protocols are needed to validate these results. Until more robust evidence becomes available, surgery should remain the preferred treatment for managing groin nodes in women with vulvar cancer. For patients who are medically unfit for surgery, primary radiotherapy may be considered as an alternative treatment option.
